title: Vibes won't cut it — Chris Kelly, Augment Code

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is AI-assisted code generation, code review as a core engineering skill, and practical workflows for coding agents in production software engineering. The speaker is from Augment Code and the entire discussion concerns IDE-integrated coding assistants and software-engineering practices. Content centers on production-grade systems with four nines uptime, serving thousands of users, and maintaining code in production. Assumes familiarity with uptime, deployment, version control, and large codebases but remains accessible to practicing engineers. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Claims are based on a practitioner's industry experience and qualitative observations, not rigorous empirical research.

summary:
Chris Kelly opens by dismissing hype-driven predictions that AI will eliminate engineering jobs within a year, arguing such claims come from people who haven't touched production systems recently. He contends AI code is still code that must run in production where complex systems exhibit emergent failures invisible at the line level. In large existing codebases, most architectural and infrastructure decisions have already been made, so generating 30% of new code offers limited leverage. He draws a historical parallel to DevOps: tractors didn't eliminate farming, they changed who does the work.

Kelly defines "vibe coding" as letting AI write and reason through code without human examination, arguing it fails for production systems requiring four nines uptime, serving thousands of users and gigabytes of data. He draws a key distinction: code is an artifact of software engineering, not the job itself—just as blueprints are an artifact of architecture. The real work involves thousands of decisions about packages, architecture, and trade-offs. Citing Jeff Atwood's "the best code is no code at all," he argues more AI-generated code is not inherently better since every line carries maintenance and debugging burden.

LLMs generate text and patterns but don't make decisions. At sufficient scale, pattern matching breaks down because production systems accumulate idiosyncrasies. Kelly defines software engineering as "changing software safely," supported by version control, testing, type systems, and deployment strategies. Augment's core thesis: context is the most important part of AI code generation.

Kelly notes current code review tools are inadequate—lexicographically sorted file lists don't reflect how software changes—and predicts an explosion in code review tooling as agents write more code. He offers practical tips for skeptical engineers: remember AI talks like a human but is a machine (it may say it "skimmed" a file, which is anthropomorphic mimicry from training data, not actual behavior); accept that LLM code may differ stylistically and use linters and style guides to settle those debates; write a rules file specifying stack and guidelines; and use a create-refine loop—generate a plan as markdown, have the agent create against it, refine, then tweak with completions. He closes expressing confidence that engineering jobs aren't going anywhere.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: AI hype skepticism and the reality of production code
sections.summary: Kelly dismisses predictions that AI will eliminate engineering jobs, arguing AI code is still code that must run in production. Large existing codebases already encode most decisions, limiting AI's leverage. He draws parallels to DevOps transformation: tractors changed farming but didn't eliminate it.

sections.title: Vibe coding vs. production requirements
sections.summary: Defines vibe coding as letting AI write code without examination. Argues it fails for production systems with four nines uptime, thousands of users, and gigabytes of data. Code is an artifact, not the job—like blueprints for an architect.

sections.title: Code as artifact; LLMs and pattern matching limits
sections.summary: Cites Jeff Atwood's 'best code is no code at all' to argue more generated code is not better. LLMs generate text and patterns but don't make decisions. At scale, pattern matching breaks down because production systems have idiosyncrasies. Vibes won't fix 2 AM outages.

sections.title: Software engineering as safe change; context and adoption
sections.summary: Defines software engineering as changing software safely. Lists traditional safeguards: knowledge, version control, testing, type systems, deployment. Augment's thesis: context is the most important part of AI code generation. Notes professional engineers are unusually slow to adopt AI.

sections.title: Tips for AI-friendly codebases and code review
sections.summary: Traces AI coding evolution from primitive tools through quality jumps to agents. Offers tips: document standards, reproducible environments, fast local testing, clear boundaries, well-defined tasks. Emphasizes AI needs the same tools engineers need. Concludes code review is the most important, underappreciated skill.

sections.title: Code review tooling, AI anthropomorphism, and practical workflow tips
sections.summary: Criticizes current code review tools as inadequate—lexicographically sorted file lists don't reflect how software changes—and predicts a tooling explosion as agents write more code. Offers practical tips: remember AI is a machine despite human-like language (it may claim to 'skim' files as anthropomorphic mimicry); accept stylistic differences in LLM code and rely on linters and style guides; write rules files with stack and guidelines; use a create-refine loop (plan as markdown, have agent create against it, refine, then tweak with completions). Closes expressing confidence that engineering jobs aren't going anywhere.
